d.title: Two nodes and a conditional edge is the whole agent
d.caption: The agent node calls the model; the conditional edge asks whether it requested a tool; the tool node runs it and the edge goes back. **Four messages for one tool round** — 3.3's 2n + 2 arithmetic, now as a graph. Everything the rest of this module adds — approval gates, trimming, step budgets, memory — is a modification to one of these two nodes or the edge between them.
d.centre: until no tool is asked for

d.title: The termination condition is the model's judgement
d.caption: `should_continue` returns `END` **when the model stops asking for tools** — so the stopping decision belongs to the model, which **is the whole idea of an agent and also 8.9's problem**: if the model never stops asking, **only the recursion limit does.** Which is why 8.9 argued for setting that limit deliberately and low on any cyclic graph: here it is not a safety net, it is the only termination guarantee in the design.

nodes.label: Only the recursion limit stops it
So it is the termination guarantee

d.title: Four places a production change lands, and you need the long form to find them
d.caption: The prebuilts replace both nodes and the graph becomes four lines of wiring — **and every production change is a change to a specific node or edge.** Each row is a modification you can only make if you know which part it belongs to. **The order is: see the long version, use the short one, unroll when a requirement demands it** — the prebuilts are the right default *and* an abstraction you will need to open.

items.label: the agent node
items.sub: a system prompt, and message trimming (9.5)

d.title: ToolNode reads the last message, so it cannot be called on its own
d.caption: It takes **state**, not arguments: it looks at the last `AIMessage`, finds its `tool_calls`, runs each one and appends a `ToolMessage` per call **with the `tool_call_id` preserved.** Which is why there is no way to invoke it directly with a tool name — **its input is the conversation, not a request** — and that is the property that makes it a graph node rather than a function.

nodes.label: So it cannot be called directly
nodes.sub: there is no request to pass

nodes.label: Which makes it a node, not a function

d.title: Order does not matter and a lost id does
d.caption: The ids are **the bookkeeping that is easy to get wrong by hand.** A provider matches each result to its request by `tool_call_id`, so **returning them in a different order is fine and losing an id is not** — the model then has a result it cannot attribute, which is 3.2's malformed-transcript failure arriving on the *next* call rather than this one. **That alone is a decent argument for the prebuilt.**

nodes.label: And it fails on the NEXT call

d.title: A raising tool becomes a ToolMessage, which is 3.7's one-try-block fix built in
d.caption: `ToolNode` catches the exception and returns its message as the `ToolMessage` content, so **the model reads what went wrong and can fix its argument or explain the problem** — which is exactly the behaviour 3.7 argued for and implemented by hand. The consequence worth noting: **a tool failure does not stop the graph.** The cycle continues, the model gets another turn, and a tool that always raises becomes a loop that the recursion limit terminates.

nodes.label: The model reads it and retries
So an always-raising tool is a loop

d.title: The router is testable on its own and the tool node is not
d.caption: `tools_condition` is a pure function of state — read the last message, return `"tools"` or `END` — so **it is testable without a graph, a model or a fixture.** `ToolNode` is not: it executes real tools. **Which is worth knowing when deciding what to cover with tests: the routing logic is the cheap, high-value test and the tool node's behaviour needs a fixture.** The hidden coupling is that `tools_condition` assumes the node is *named* `"tools"`.

nodes.label: So rename the node and routing breaks

d.title: The whole agent, in four lines of wiring
d.caption: Two prebuilts and three edges. **What was 9.1's forty lines is now four** — and the reason 9.1 wrote it out first is visible here: **this version has no place to put a step budget, a system prompt or an approval gate**, because the nodes it would attach to are inside the prebuilts. Which is the honest summary of prebuilts throughout this course: **right as a default, and the first thing a real requirement makes you unroll.**

nodes.label: And nowhere to put a budget or a gate

d.title: Prompt chaining is a chain, and wanting the steps named is not a reason for a graph
d.caption: Three model calls in a fixed order with each output feeding the next — **which is a chain, so 8.1's rule applies and a graph adds nothing.** The exception is stated precisely: **if you need a gate between the steps, that is a reason to use a graph. Wanting the steps named is not.** Which is the most common bad reason in this module, because a graph does give you names and 2.9's `run_name` gives you the same thing on a chain.

nodes.label: Need a gate between steps?
nodes.sub: a real reason for a graph

nodes.label: 2.9's run_name does that on a chain

d.title: Routing in a graph is 2.5's router with the destinations visible
d.caption: A classifier node plus a conditional edge does what 2.5's `RunnableLambda` returning a Runnable did — **and the difference is that the destinations are in the graph rather than inside a function.** So the drawing shows every branch, 8.7's path map keeps the decision topology-independent, and the router is a pure function you can test. **The cost is the schema and the wiring**, which is 8.6's four-lines-against-one comparison again.

nodes.label: A conditional edge with a path map
So the drawing shows every branch
At the cost of a schema and wiring

d.title: The reducer on the shared key is mandatory, not optional
d.caption: **8.6's superstep model applies in full: all three branches see the same snapshot, none can observe another, and the reducer on the shared findings key is mandatory rather than optional** — without one the fan-in **raises** `InvalidUpdateError`, which 8.3 measured. Which makes parallelisation the pattern that forces you to understand reducers: you cannot build it and discover the requirement later, because it will not run.

nodes.label: You cannot discover it later
nodes.sub: it will not run at all

d.title: The orchestrator decides how many workers, which a fixed fan-out cannot
d.caption: **It needs 8.7's list-returning router**: the orchestrator produced three sections, so three workers ran. **A statically wired fan-out would have had to guess that number** — and guessing high wastes calls on sections that do not exist while guessing low drops work. Which is the first pattern in this lesson where the graph is doing something a chain genuinely cannot, rather than doing the same thing with more machinery.

nodes.label: The first pattern a chain cannot do

d.title: Evaluator-optimiser is a cycle with a condition, so the iteration count is runtime
d.caption: Generate, evaluate, and loop back if the evaluation says to. **Which makes the iteration count a runtime property** — so, like the orchestrator, this needs a graph rather than wanting one. And it inherits the agent's termination problem in a milder form: **the loop ends when the evaluator is satisfied, so an evaluator that is never satisfied is bounded only by the recursion limit.**

d.title: Six patterns, sorted by who holds control and whether the paths are enumerable
d.caption: **The enumerable column is the one that decides how you test and budget.** The first three have control in your code and **exactly enumerable paths** — so you can assert on the path, bound the cost and draw the graph completely. The last three take their shape from runtime, and the agent row is the honest end of it: **control is the model's and nothing is bounded**, which is 3.8's p95 and 8.9's recursion limit in one line.

d.title: An 8 KB blob in the state is 24 KB written for a two-node run
d.caption: Without the blob, a two-node run writes **88 bytes across four checkpoints**. With an 8 KB field in the schema it writes **24,062 bytes** — because **the whole state is serialised at every superstep**, so the blob is paid for once per step rather than once. Which is 8.4's argument for the three-schema split, measured: **keeping a large value out of the state schema is the only thing that helps, and an output schema does not.**

d.title: The reducer appends to the persisted list, so the second run includes the first
d.caption: Invoking the same `thread_id` again **continues from the persisted state**, and the important detail is what that does to an accumulating key: **the reducer appends to the *persisted* list, so the second run's history includes the first.** Which is correct for a conversation and surprising for anything else — a `trace` key accumulating across runs is the same mechanism producing something nobody wanted, and nothing distinguishes the two cases.

nodes.label: The reducer appends to the persisted list

d.title: Three savers, and the default survives nothing
d.caption: **`InMemorySaver` holds checkpoints in a Python dict, so a redeploy, a crash or a second worker process all produce an empty result — and the code is unchanged, so nothing indicates a problem.** Which is exactly what a process restart looks like from the outside: memory that worked in development and does not in production, with no error and no diff. The concurrent-readers column is the one that bites at the second worker rather than the first restart.

d.title: A thread_id with no checkpointer is accepted and does nothing
d.caption: Passing `thread_id` **without** a checkpointer is **accepted** — the run completes normally and persists nothing. So the configuration that looks like memory is memory-shaped and empty, and **the only symptom is that the second turn does not remember the first**, which reads as a model problem rather than a missing argument. 9.5 adds the sharper version: **a system that remembers nothing cannot leak anything, so this bug hides the two security bugs in that lesson during testing.**

nodes.label: The symptom is 'it does not remember'
nodes.sub: which reads as a model problem

nodes.label: And it hides 9.5's leaks in testing

d.title: The whole state is thread-scoped, and two of these three want something else
d.caption: **There is no per-thread and per-user distinction inside the state** — the whole thing is scoped to the `thread_id`. Which is correct for conversation history and **wrong for the other two rows**: a user's preferences are **forgotten when a new conversation starts**, and a cached lookup is **recomputed once per thread.** Neither is a bug in the mechanism; both are the mechanism being asked to hold something whose lifetime is different, which is what 9.6's store is for.

d.title: Nothing validates a thread_id, so the boundary has to be an authorisation decision
d.caption: **It is a dictionary key.** So a `thread_id` taken from the request body lets a caller read any conversation whose id they can guess or enumerate. **The fix is to derive it server-side from the authenticated session and never from the request body, which makes the boundary an authorisation decision rather than a parameter.** And the third failure is 9.4's, which is **the opposite bug — the leak is absent and so is the memory — and it hides the other two during testing.**

nodes.label: Now it is an authorisation decision
And 9.4's bug hides both in testing

d.title: Memory working correctly and storage growing quadratically are the same mechanism
d.caption: Six turns gives **12 messages in state and 13 checkpoints for the thread** — and because the whole state is written at every superstep, **the storage is the sum of a growing list written once per step.** `add_messages` appends and **nothing removes anything**, so the growth is not a leak to find; it is the feature. **Which is why trimming is not an optional optimisation** — there is no setting that bounds this.

d.title: Two trimming strategies, and both are nodes you can get wrong
d.caption: **Both are nodes in the graph, which means they are also places where a decision gets made and can be got wrong.** Keeping the last N loses the beginning — **including anything the user said once and expects to be remembered.** Summarising uses 8.3's **id-based replacement** in `add_messages`, because you are editing history rather than appending to it. And the detail that makes the naive version fail: **a trimming node that drops a tool call but keeps its `ToolMessage` leaves the history malformed**, so trimming has to respect message pairing.

cells.text: the beginning - said once, expected remembered

cells: and it must respect message pairing

cells.text: needs id-based replacement, not an append

d.title: Five properties, and the written row is the one with a cost
d.caption: The store is not a nicer state — **it is state with a different lifetime and a different write cost.** The row that matters operationally is the fourth: **graph state is written every superstep and a store is written when you call `put`**, so 9.4's 8 KB blob costs 8 KB per step in state and 8 KB once in a store. And the read row is the trade going the other way: state arrives automatically and a store has to be read **explicitly, by key**, which means you have to know what you are looking for.

d.title: Three kinds of memory, distinguished by how they are retrieved
d.caption: The useful distinction is not what they contain but **how you get them back.** Semantic facts are retrieved **by key, or by embedding search over the values**. Episodic records are retrieved **by recency, or by similarity to the current situation** — which is module 5's machinery pointed at your own history. And procedural instructions are **always loaded and injected into the system prompt**, so they are not retrieved at all — which also makes them the only kind with an unbounded prompt cost.
cells: key, or embedding search over values

cells.text: always loaded - so it costs prompt tokens

d.title: Namespace design decides what you can retrieve without a scan
d.caption: Layout A puts everything in one namespace with the user encoded in the key: **`search(('memories',))` returns all three items — every user's — and getting just alice's means filtering in your own code.** Layout B puts the user in the namespace, so the same question is a namespace read. **The retrieval pattern is fixed at write time by a decision that looks like naming**, and changing it later means rewriting every key.

steps.code: and it is fixed at write time

d.title: The API is four methods; deciding what is worth remembering is the problem
d.caption: **No part of the interface addresses what to remember — it is a product and prompt-design problem that happens to have a storage layer.** And the three failures are not symmetrical. **Remember everything** fills the store with noise and **retrieval returns irrelevant memories — 6.6's near-duplicate problem, with no relevance labels to tune against.** Remember nothing is a feature nobody notices. And **remember wrong persists a mistaken fact across every future conversation**, which is the only one of the three that gets worse with time.

items.label: Remember everything
items.sub: noise, and 6.6's problem with no labels to tune against

items.label: Remember wrong
items.sub: a mistaken fact in every future conversation - and it compounds
